title: Traffic seeding strategies and repeatable bench playbook
content:
Purpose and scope
This note collects practical seeding/priming strategies and a playbook to improve throughput-benchmark repeatability across hosts, GPUs, and model variants. It focuses on reducing stochastic noise during loadgen runs and on deterministic steps to get steady-state measurements that are comparable run-to-run.

Why this matters
- Small variation in early tokens, kernel JIT, or NVidia driver behavior can change throughput percentiles enough to mislead optimization decisions.
- We need a short, reproducible checklist that scripts can run before a benchmark to: 1) reach stable KV/cache state, 2) eliminate one-off kernel/JIT stalls, and 3) ensure client-side pacing is not a hidden source of noise.

Principles we follow
- Separate concerns: client pacing, model priming, runtime priming, and OS-level repeatability. Triage noise to the layer where it originates.
- Prefer simple deterministic seeds for stochastic components (load RNG, request order, synthetic variation).
- Make warmup short but effective — avoid long arbitrary ramps that burn capacity without targeting sources of non-repeatability.
- Capture and archive raw per-request timing traces and environment dumps for each run.

Quick playbook (executable checklist)
1) Environment snapshot (before anything):
   - Record driver versions (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version --format=csv), CUDA, cudNN, container runtime, kernel version.
   - Dump NVML config and MIG partitioning (if used).
   - Pin CPU and IRQ affinity for inference processes where feasible.
2) Deterministic client configuration:
   - Use explicit RNG seed for request ordering and any synthetic tokenization noise.
   - Fix concurrency schedule in a YAML file. No randomized jitter unless testing burstiness.
   - Use fixed prompt sets with token length distribution representative of target workload. Archive the prompt file used for each run.
3) Model & runtime priming sequence (fast targeted priming):
   - Load model once; perform an ordered set of 3–5 warmup calls with growing sequence length: short (16 tokens), medium (64 tokens), long (256 tokens).
   - Immediately run an additional pass using the same prompts but with batch_size=1 to exercise per-request overhead (kernel path).
   - If using quantized kernels, run a targeted token-stepping loop to populate KV cache and any per-layer caches (recommended 10–20 inputs with realistic prefixes).
4) Kernel/JIT stabilization:
   - For runtimes that JIT or select kernels adaptively, include a dedicated warmup that covers the heavy-attention shapes used in the benchmark.
   - For Triton/Flash-attention builds: run an isolated micro-benchmark of the attention kernel with the same seq_len and batch shapes for 30–60s.
5) Client pacing & measurement:
   - Use a fixed-rate pacing loop with token-based backpressure: do not issue next request until prior has acknowledged reception of first token if streaming is used.
   - Sample latencies at the token level (time-to-first-token, per-token delta) in addition to request-level metrics.
6) Steady-state detection:
   - Define steady-state as 3 consecutive 60-second windows with mean throughput variation < 2% and p95 latency within target range.
   - If steady-state is not reached within a configurable timeout (e.g., 10 minutes), mark run as unstable and archive traces for investigation.
7) Run packing and artifacts:
   - Run N replicates (N=5 recommended) with identical config files. Do not reuse the same process without restarting the runtime to catch process-level drift.
   - Save: environment snapshot, prompt list, loadgen config, per-request trace CSV, summary histograms, and a condensed run.json with top-level stats.

Advanced techniques and rationales
- Synthetic trace replay: record a realistic production sampling (timestamps + token counts) and replay it deterministically with a seeded client. This helps reproduce temporal patterns without introducing RNG noise.
- Sequence-length occupancy conditioning: if the model has heavy variance in sequence lengths, run stratified bench segments per bucket (0-32, 33-128, 129-512) and compute weighted aggregate throughput. This avoids misleading averages caused by rare long sequences.
- KV-first request ordering: when evaluating KV/cache effectiveness, prime caches by issuing a set of prefix-only requests that populate KV cache, then run throughput tests. Compare against cold-start baseline.
- Kernel concurrency isolation: pin the inference process to dedicated cores, and isolate non-critical system daemons (disable cron jobs, snapshot tasks) to reduce OS jitter.

Concrete loadgen YAML snippet (example, include in archived artifacts):

# loadgen example (literal; keep in artifact archive)
# seed and schedule fixed, sequence buckets defined
seed: 1337
concurrency: 32
schedule:
  - duration_s: 60
    rps: 0
    mode: warmup
  - duration_s: 300
    rps: 1200
    mode: steady
prompts_file: "prompts/bench_prompts_v2.txt"
sequence_buckets:
  - max_tokens: 32
    weight: 0.6
  - max_tokens: 128
    weight: 0.3
  - max_tokens: 512
    weight: 0.1
token_backpressure: true

(Ensure this YAML is committed with run metadata.)

Common failure modes and how to debug them
- Symptom: p99s spike only during first minute of steady window. Cause: incomplete JIT coverage or late kernel selection. Fix: extend targeted kernel micro-run.
- Symptom: run-to-run throughput swings >5% despite identical configs. Cause: transient OS scheduling or background jobs. Fix: re-run with CPU isolation and collect perf top samples during run.
- Symptom: batching behavior changes throughput unexpectedly with same latency budget. Cause: batcher warmup/flush thresholds. Fix: run controlled microbench with fixed batch shapes and verify batcher logs.

Reporting template (for each experiment)
- Config name (link):
- Host snapshot id:
- GPU/Driver/CUDA:
- Loadgen seed:
- Prompts file:
- Warmup steps performed:
- Replicates run: N
- Aggregate metrics: mean throughput, std, p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies (token-level and request-level)
- Notes on anomalies and follow-ups

Automation notes (for runners and CI)
- Runner should enforce a fresh runtime restart between replicates to capture process cold/steady transitions.
- Use a sidecar collector to stream per-token traces to a compact binary (protocol buffer) to avoid overloaded clients during high RPS.
- Add a regression check that fails CI if mean throughput drops >3% from a pinned baseline for a model variant.

Open questions / experiments to try next
- How much do MIG slices change priming behavior? (run stratified tests by MIG partition)
- Optimal number of targeted kernel micro-runs for different model families (Llama2-style vs. transformer-mixture).
- Can we safely reduce replicates to N=3 for faster cycles if we add adaptive early stopping when variance is low?

Appendix: minimal artifact checklist to publish with results
- commit sha of runtime and model
- host snapshot (uname -a, nvidia-smi output)
- prompts file and tokenization stats
- loadgen YAML and binary used
- archived per-request CSV and aggregated histograms

Notes to self: keep this playbook as the canonical lightweight priming procedure for throughput experiments. If a benchmark requires special treatment (e.g., streaming-only or function-calling heavy), make a branch of this checklist that documents the extra steps.
